summary_md: Hargrave and Blumenau (UCL working paper; the text is dated October 2021, filed here as 2022) track how gendered debating style changed in the UK House of Commons between May 1997 and March 2019. The corpus is 418,147 MP-debate observations: 1,422 MPs across 14,864 debates. They score eight styles. Three are communal: human narrative, affect and positive emotion. Five are agentic: fact, complexity, repetition, aggression and negative emotion. Six of the measures come from seed dictionaries expanded with GloVe embeddings, and these beat standard dictionaries against human coding for every style except fact (positive emotion about 0.70 against 0.38). Each style goes through a Bayesian dynamic hierarchical model with debate random effects, so gender gaps are estimated within debates. Early in the period, women used more communal styles and men more aggression and complexity. Women also used more fact, repetition and negative emotion, which runs against the stereotype. For six of eight styles the share of between-MP variation explained by gender fell, by 29 to 60 percent comparing the periods before and after 2007. Fact and negative emotion went the other way, rising to about 4 and 9 percent of MP-level variation after 2007. The change sits mostly with women, whose communal styles declined. The work is observational and does not separate mechanisms. For Paul's systems, the main point is that agency, communion and negative-emotion text scores can carry a gender signature that changes over time. The persona channel and affective N in the receptivity layer check for a party signature but not for gender. This is UK floor debate measured with dictionaries, not the US Congress, so any transfer is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.

bearings.paper_claim: Communal styles (human narrative, affect, positive emotion) were higher among female MPs early in 1997-2019, and the gap shrank to no consistent difference by recent sessions. For converging styles, gender's share of between-MP style variation fell 29-60 percent comparing pre-2007 with post-2007. Window: UK Commons 1997-2019; denominator: MP-by-session variation from the hierarchical model.
bearings.system_side: persona_z = .60 z(communion) - .40 z(agency) from LLM cue shares. It is blended into susceptibility at PERSONA_W 0.30 for members with 15 or more classified sentences. The only demographic check recorded is a party signature (communion D .099 vs R .049). No gender check exists. By contrast, cooperation_v2 and reactivity were both checked gender-clean.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfer holds only if US House and Senate rhetoric shows a gender gap in communion or agency cue shares. The paper uses embedding dictionaries over all speech, while the system uses LLM classification of self-referential cue sentences (Birkenmaier codebook), which is a different construct operationalisation. A one-shot check is to correlate persona_susc_z with the legislators.csv gender column, partialled on party. Any result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Negative emotion runs against the stereotype: women use more of it than men for much of the period. The gap diverged, with gender explaining about 2 percent of MP-level variation in 1997-2007 and about 9 percent after 2007. Divergence comes almost entirely from differential replacement of MPs, not from within-MP change.
bearings.system_side: affective_n is an LLM affective-facet sum (pessimism, anxiety, depression, volatility) from interview text, residualized on E and then on party, and z-scored. The LIWC i + negemo - posemo composite is kept only as a convergent anchor (r +.24). There is no gender residualization or gender audit. The components.txt row still describes LIWC as an additive component, which is stale against the code.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies if US members' negative-affect expression differs by gender in the interview genre. The paper's negative-emotion measure is a dictionary score on UK floor speech, and the interview genre already failed genre transfer in this system (rho .050, .161). The paper also suggests the composition of the chamber can move any gender loading, so a check would need a stated window.

bearings.paper_claim: Seed dictionaries expanded with GloVe word embeddings (150 dimensions, window 3, TF-IDF weighted sentence scores) correlate with human coder judgements at about 0.61-0.85 per style. Standard dictionaries do worse, e.g. positive emotion 0.38 and 0.34 against 0.70 and 0.71 for the embedding measure, roughly 70 comparisons per style.
bearings.paper_location: p.15-17; Table S4 p.S17; p.S19; S2-S7
bearings.system_side: Closed-vocabulary posemo, negemo, anx and anger rates use short published-exemplar word lists (about 20-30 words each) unless licensed LIWC .dic files are dropped in. The rates are z-scored and enter only through fitted SMOreg weights.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a route to better emotion-category rates on congressional text (embedding expansion from seed words, validated against a small human-coded sample). It would change trait inputs, so it falls under change control and a single-look discipline. The paper's validation covers UK debate sentences, not US floor speech or interviews.

gaps_exposed: No gender audit exists for the persona channel (persona_susc_z) or for affective_n, although cooperation_v2, reactivity and voice ES were all checked against gender. legislators.csv carries a gender column, so a party-partialled check is cheap.

Psychometric text scores are corpus-relative z with no control for topic or debate context. The paper estimates style gaps within debates (debate random effects), while the system cannot separate a member's style from the topics or venues they speak in.

The persona channel assumes communal rhetoric signals approachability and susceptibility. The paper shows stereotype-linked style is time-varying and driven by chamber composition, so a static communal-means-susceptible prior may drift. Nothing in the system re-checks the prior over time.
Emotion categories in big5_traits.py use short exemplar lists with no human-coded validation sample on congressional text.
flags: Metadata: the text is dated October 08, 2021, while the vault slug and hint say 2022. The venue is a UCL working paper.
components.txt describes affective_n as z(LIWC) + z(LLM). The live code (emit_affective_n.py:39-56) uses the LLM facets only, with LIWC as a convergent anchor, so the component row is stale.

Any gender-residualization suggestion drawn from this paper is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). Changing receptivity inputs is not recommended here, only checking them.
No conflict with the SNA rejections (D-021, D-025, D-104..D-108). The paper has no network content.
paul_alignment: No Paul annotations or entries exist for this work (0 markup, 0 dropped). The closest of Paul's positions is on persona-agency-communion, built on Birkenmaier and Lechner 2025: codebooks and node design, with his concerns being the conversion from trait to node and ambiguous statements. This paper adds a concern Paul's notes do not raise, namely that agency and communion text scores can encode gender and that the encoding shifts over time. This sharpens his trait-to-node worry, since PERSONA_W 0.30 may partly carry gender. His note is not stale, only silent on demographic confounds.

related.why: Both measure agency and communion in politicians' text. Birkenmaier uses LLM cue classification, which is the system's persona instrument, while Hargrave and Blumenau use embedding-expanded dictionaries for style and add the gender and time dimension.
The PoliPers framework defines the agency and communion codebook the system uses. Hargrave and Blumenau supply evidence on how those poles map onto gendered expectations.
Cited for emotive rhetoric in parliaments. It is the same Westminster debate setting with a different emotion target.
Corpus-based dictionary expansion for specialised vocabularies (cited as Rice and Zorn 2021). It is the method family behind the paper's embedding-expanded seed dictionaries.
Also builds embedding-based emotion lexicons for Westminster parliamentary debate. Together they give two routes to domain-adapted emotion scores.

Standard closed dictionaries in the LIWC tradition are the benchmark the paper beats on human-coded validity (positive emotion 0.38 against 0.70), which challenges direct reuse of generic emotion categories on parliamentary text.
This is the US Congress analogue of emotional expression in legislative speech. It is the venue where any transfer of the UK gender-style findings would need checking.
Infers elite traits from speech with closed vocabulary, while this paper shows such style scores carry demographic and temporal structure that trait readings should control for.
